960.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
960.hook: Martin Luther King Jr, jailed, writes to fellow clergy that injustice in one place threatens justice in every place
960.howItsDone: Some Christians read King's letter in churches, classrooms and study groups, and some congregations read parts of it aloud together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Billy Graham, an old hymn, and ropes coming down. Your line was just as I am. Who did you invite, and did they come? Day nine hundred sixty.

A cell in the Birmingham city jail. A pastor has been arrested for leading a march in defiance of a court order. Someone brings him a newspaper, and in it is a public statement from a group of white clergymen in the city. They call the demonstrations unwise and untimely. They say outsiders are stirring up trouble, and the right course is patience and the courts. The pastor has no desk and not much paper. The story goes that he starts writing his answer in the margins of that very newspaper, and on scraps smuggled in and out. The pastor is Martin Luther King Jr., and he is writing to fellow ministers. Today, his letter.

King wrote as a minister to ministers, and the letter is full of the Bible and the church. To the charge that he was an outsider, he answered that he was in Birmingham because injustice was there. He compared himself to the apostle Paul, who left his home town to carry the gospel to other cities. And then he made a claim readers still quote: injustice in one place is a threat to justice in every place. In his picture, all people are bound together in a single garment of destiny, so a tear in one part runs through the whole cloth. What happens to one city happens, in the end, to everyone. To the charge that the time wasn't right, he wrote that for Black Americans the word wait had nearly always meant never. And to the question of breaking laws, he reached back to Augustine and Thomas Aquinas, saints of the church, to argue that an unjust law is no true law at all, while insisting that anyone who breaks one must do it openly, lovingly, and accept the penalty. He also reached for the prophet Amos. In the King James Bible, Amos says: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Not a trickle, saved for a better season. A river. Some of the letter's sharpest words aren't aimed at open enemies. They're aimed at the white moderate, who agrees with the goal in principle and keeps asking for patience, and at white churches that stood by. King wrote with grief about the church, not against it. He was a pastor, disappointed in his own house, and he still called it home.

Here's the practice: speak for justice somewhere. Settle, and breathe. Think of one unfairness close to you that isn't happening to you. A coworker always talked over. A neighbor without a ramp. A rule at school that lands harder on some kids than others. Don't solve it yet. Just look at it plainly, and notice the part of you that wants to say it's not the right time. Then choose one small, honest word you could say, to whom, and when. If you pray, you can hold Amos's line about justice running down like water. The bell holds the time.
Letter from Birmingham Jail. Martin Luther King Jr.'s answer, from a cell, to fellow clergy who had told him to wait.
Your line: justice is all one piece. Today, say the one honest word you chose, kindly and clearly, about an unfairness that isn't yours. Day nine hundred sixty.

961.title: The mountaintop
961.hook: the night before he is killed, King says he's seen the promised land
961.howItsDone: Some churches in the United States remember King's life and words near his birthday, and the mountaintop speech is sometimes played or read aloud at those services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Letter from Birmingham Jail, written in the margins. Your line was justice is all one piece. Did you say your one honest word? Day nine hundred sixty-one.

Rain and wind outside a church in Memphis. Sanitation workers in the city are on strike, carrying signs that say they are men, and Martin Luther King Jr. has come to stand with them. He's tired. He has a sore throat. He nearly stays at the hotel, but the people waiting call him, and he comes. He speaks for a long time, about the strike, about the Good Samaritan, about the road ahead. Then, near the end, he starts to talk about his own life and how long it might be. The next evening, he is shot and killed on a motel balcony. Today, the last thing he told that crowd.

In the closing minutes of the speech, King said that he had been to the mountaintop. He said he had looked over and seen the promised land. He might not get there with them, he said, but he wanted them to know that they, as a people, would get there. And he said that he wasn't worried, and that he feared no one. Listeners who knew their Bibles would have heard where those words came from. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses has led his people out of slavery and through the wilderness. He climbs a mountain, to the top of Pisgah, and God shows him the whole land spread out below. Then God says, in the King James Bible: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." Moses sees it. He doesn't enter it. He dies there, and the people go on without him. King placed himself in that story. That is not a hopeless story. The letter to the Hebrews describes the old heroes of faith the same way: "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them." Seeing from far off is still seeing. Hope, in this picture, doesn't depend on getting there yourself. King ended that night with the opening line of the Battle Hymn of the Republic: "Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord." Then he stepped back from the pulpit. Some listeners remember the speech for its strange calm. A man who sounds as if he senses what may be coming, and has made his peace with not crossing over.
screen: `MOSES ON PISGAH: SEE, BUT NOT ENTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look ahead with hope. Settle, and breathe. Think of something good you are part of that you may never see finished. A child growing up. A garden. A cause. A family healing slowly. A church, a team, a town. Picture it from a height, the way Moses saw the land. Not the mess of today. The whole of it, further on, the way you hope it will be. Let yourself see it from far off, without needing to arrive. If you pray, you can offer it to God as unfinished. The bell holds the time.
The mountaintop. King's last speech, in Memphis, where he said he had seen the promised land and might not get there with his people.

Your line: look toward the promised land. Today, do one small thing for a future you may never see: plant something, teach something, or leave a place better for whoever comes next. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

962.title: Fannie Lou Hamer
962.hook: a sharecropper beaten for registering voters sings This Little Light of Mine
962.howItsDone: Black churches in the United States sing This Little Light of Mine in worship, and it was sung at mass meetings and marches of the civil rights movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mountaintop, and Moses seeing a land he would not enter. Your line was look toward the promised land. What did you do for a future you may not see? Day nine hundred sixty-two.

A bus full of tired people is rolling back from a county courthouse in Mississippi. They have just tried to register to vote, and been turned away. Police stop the bus on a made-up charge. Fear goes through the seats like a draft. And then one woman, a sharecropper who has spent long years in the cotton fields, starts to sing. A church song. Others join in. That woman is Fannie Lou Hamer. That evening the plantation owner tells her to take back her registration or leave. She leaves. Today, a woman who kept singing.

Hamer grew up in the Mississippi Delta, in a family of sharecroppers, and she grew up in church. When young organizers came through asking Black citizens to register to vote, she raised her hand. It cost her the home and the work she had. It cost her more later. Coming back from a voter workshop, she and others were arrested in the town of Winona, and in that jail she was beaten so badly she carried the injuries for the rest of her life. She didn't stop. She sang. Her song was This Little Light of Mine, a gospel song sung in Black churches, and she sang it on buses, in mass meetings, outside courthouses, and, people remember, in jail. The song echoes a saying of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount. In the King James Bible: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." And then: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house." A bushel was a basket for measuring grain. Nobody lights a lamp and puts a basket over it. Hamer's little light was not small in the end. She told her story to a committee of a national political convention, on television, and asked out loud whether this was the country it claimed to be. She is remembered for saying she was tired of being tired. She also spoke of loving the people who hurt her, because her faith asked it, and she said so plainly. A small light, in her life, meant one voice that would not go back under the basket.

Here's the practice: sing a small light song. Settle, and breathe. If you know This Little Light of Mine, hum it quietly, or sing one line under your breath. If you know another song about light, use that. If singing isn't for you, light a candle, or switch on a lamp, and just watch it for a while. Notice how a small flame fills a dark room. Then think of one good thing you've been keeping under a basket. If you pray, you can hold Jesus's words: ye are the light of the world. The bell holds the time.
Fannie Lou Hamer. A Mississippi sharecropper who lost her home and was beaten for registering to vote, and kept singing This Little Light of Mine.
Your line: this little light. Today, take one good thing out from under the basket and let it be seen, not for praise, but so it gives light to the house. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

963.title: Vatican II (1962–65)
963.hook: the Catholic Church opens its windows: Mass in local languages, new respect for other churches
963.howItsDone: Catholic parishes today celebrate Mass in local languages, with readings from both Testaments, while some parishes also celebrate the older Latin form.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fannie Lou Hamer, singing on a stopped bus. Your line was this little light. What did you take out from under the basket? Day nine hundred sixty-three.

A small book with a ribbon in it, worn soft at the corners. It's an old Catholic missal, and on each page the prayers of the Mass run in two columns: Latin on one side, the local language on the other. For a long time, Catholics of the Western church heard the Mass in Latin, whether they lived in Manila or Milwaukee, and followed along in books like this one. Then a pope, John the Twenty-Third, called the bishops of the world to Rome for a council. A story often told has him opening a window to show what he hoped it would do: let in fresh air. Today, the council that came of it.

The Second Vatican Council met in Rome over several autumns, and the bishops wrote a set of documents that changed ordinary church life. Take four of them in turn. First, worship. The council allowed the Mass to be said in local languages, and asked that the people take a full, active part in it, not only watch. Soon parishes around the world were hearing the prayers in their own tongue. Some Catholics heard in this an echo of Pentecost in the book of Acts, where, in the King James Bible, "every man heard them speak in his own language." Second, scripture. The council urged that the Bible be opened wide to ordinary Catholics, read, prayed and studied, not left to the clergy. Third, other Christians. The council spoke of Protestant and Orthodox Christians with new warmth, as brothers and sisters in Christ, still separated, and called Catholics to pray and work for unity. Fourth, other faiths. In a short document, the council said that the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions. And it said plainly that the death of Christ cannot be charged against all the Jews of his time, or against Jews today, and it deplored hatred of Jews. Catholics still discuss how to read the council. Some see a long-overdue renewal. Some feel that beauty and reverence were lost along the way, and some parishes still celebrate the older Latin Mass with permission. Both groups are reading the same documents. That is part of what a council leaves behind.
screen: `RESPECT FOR OTHER FAITHS, AND FOR JEWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one thing Vatican II changed. Settle, and breathe. Choose one of the four: the language of worship, the Bible in ordinary hands, other Christians, other faiths. Sit with it. If you're Catholic, think about the next Mass you'll attend, and the words you'll hear in your own language. If you're not, think about what it would be like to hear the prayers at the center of someone's week in a language they understood, or didn't. If you pray, you can pray in whatever words are truly yours. The bell holds the time.
Vatican II. The Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council, which brought the Mass into local languages and spoke with new respect of other churches and faiths.
Your line: open the windows. Today, open one: to a person, an idea, or a church you've kept at arm's length. Just let some air in. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

964.title: Lifting the anathemas (1965)
964.hook: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lift the mutual excommunications from the old split between East and West
964.howItsDone: Delegations from Rome and from the patriarchate in Istanbul now visit each other on their churches' patronal feast days, and official dialogue between the two churches continues.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vatican II, and a pope who wanted fresh air in the church. Your line was open the windows. Which window did you open, even a crack? Day nine hundred sixty-four.

Two churches, one statement, read aloud on the same day in two cities. In Rome, at the end of the council, in front of the bishops. In Istanbul, the old Constantinople, in the patriarch's church. The statement is about something that happened long before anyone in either room was born. Back at the time of the great split between the Christian East and the Christian West, envoys from Rome and the patriarch in Constantinople had pronounced sentences of excommunication on each other. Those sentences had sat on the record ever since, like a door slammed and never reopened. Now Pope Paul the Sixth and Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople agree to lift them. Today, two churches saying sorry.

An anathema is a solemn curse or ban, a sentence that puts someone outside the church. The word is in the New Testament. When Paul writes to the Galatians about anyone who preaches a different gospel, the King James Bible gives it as "let him be accursed." Strong words, meant for serious cases. The story usually told of the old split runs like this. Envoys from Rome, in Constantinople, laid a document of excommunication on the altar of the great church there, and walked out. The patriarch and his synod answered with excommunications of their own. The quarrel had many roots, theology, authority, language, politics, and those sentences became a symbol of all of it. Then two men decided to act. Paul and Athenagoras had already met and embraced in Jerusalem. Now they issued a joint declaration. In it they said they regretted the offensive words and the hurtful actions of that time, and they asked that the sentences be removed from memory and from the midst of the church, consigned to oblivion. What it did not do matters too. It did not restore full communion. The two churches still do not celebrate the Eucharist together, and their dialogue continues, with patience, on both sides. The declaration itself says this gesture is not enough to end the differences. It was a start. Jesus put the order of things plainly, in the King James Bible: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." The story goes that the old sentence from Rome was laid on an altar. The undoing began when both sides laid it aside.

Here's the practice: undo one old grudge. Settle, and breathe. Let one old grudge come to mind. Not the biggest one. A medium one. A cousin, an old friend, a former boss. Notice how long you've kept it on the record. Notice what it costs you to keep it there. You don't have to make up with them today. A pope and a patriarch didn't fix everything in one statement either. Just ask: what would it mean to lift the sentence, even if nothing else changes yet? If you pray, you can bring Jesus's words about leaving the gift at the altar. The bell holds the time.
anathema. Greek for a solemn curse, the old sentences of excommunication that Pope Paul the Sixth and Patriarch Athenagoras set aside between Rome and Constantinople.
Your line: nine hundred years undone. Today, take one step on an old grudge: a short message, a kind word, or simply deciding to stop rehearsing it. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

fork.reveal: Paul and Athenagoras lifted the sentences together and said the gesture was not enough on its own. the deeper questions are still being worked through.

965.title: Taizé
965.hook: Brother Roger's community in France welcomes young people from every church to sing and pray
965.howItsDone: Churches of different traditions hold Taizé-style evening prayers with short repeated chants, candles, scripture and silence, and young people travel to Taizé for a week of prayer and community life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lifting the anathemas, a pope and a patriarch setting down old sentences. Your line was nine hundred years undone. Did you set down a grudge, even for an hour? Day nine hundred sixty-five.

Evening in a long, low church on a hill in the French countryside. No pews. Young people sit on the floor, on their knees, on little wooden stools, packed close. Candles. Orange cloth. Then a single short line is sung, and sung again, and again, until it isn't a song anymore so much as a kind of breathing. Then it changes language. Then, in the middle of the prayer, everything stops, and there is a long silence that nobody fills. Some of the people in that room are Catholic, some Protestant, some Orthodox, and some aren't sure what they are. Today, the village where this happens.

The story begins with one man. Roger Schutz was a young Swiss Protestant who came to the village of Taizé, in Burgundy, during the Second World War. He bought a house close to the line that divided France, and he sheltered refugees there, among them Jews fleeing the Nazis. When the house was in danger, he had to leave. After the war he came back, and other men joined him. They became a community of brothers, living together under vows, praying together through the day. In time the brothers came from Protestant backgrounds and from the Catholic Church, all living one life. Then young people started showing up. They came to pray, to talk, to work, and to sleep in tents and simple barracks. And they kept coming, from many countries and many churches. The brothers wrote songs for them that anyone could join: a single line, often from scripture or an old prayer, repeated until it sinks in. One of them uses an old Latin hymn: "Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est." Where charity and love are, God is there. The brothers don't try to start a new church or move anyone from theirs. They send people home, to their own parish, their own congregation. The prayer there is meant to carry the joy of the gospel, a joy that doesn't depend on things going well. It sounds like the angel's announcement in Luke, in the King James Bible: "I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." To all people. In a village in Burgundy, the door stays open to whoever comes.

Here's the practice: sing a Taizé chant, or the spirit of one. Settle, and breathe. Take one short line and repeat it slowly, sung, hummed or just spoken. You could use the old Latin, ubi caritas, where charity and love are, God is there. Or the words of the thief beside Jesus on the cross, which one Taizé chant sets to music, from Luke: Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. Let the line go round and round until you stop thinking about it. Then let it fall away into silence. The bell holds the time.
Taizé. A village in France where Brother Roger's community of brothers from different churches welcomes young people to sing short chants and pray in silence.
Your line: the joy of the gospel. Today, let one short line of good news repeat in you while you work, and notice where it brings a little joy. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

966.title: Oscar Romero
966.hook: an archbishop in El Salvador speaks for the poor and is shot while saying Mass
966.howItsDone: The Catholic calendar marks Saint Oscar Romero's feast on the day of his death, and pilgrims visit the hospital chapel in San Salvador where he was killed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Taizé, one short line sung until it became breathing. Your line was the joy of the gospel. Which line kept repeating in you? Day nine hundred sixty-six.

A list of names, read aloud from the pulpit of the cathedral in San Salvador on a Sunday morning. Before it, the archbishop has read the gospel and explained it. Now he reads out the news of the week. People taken from their homes. People found dead by the road. Priests, farmers, students. Across the country, in shops and farmhouses and city apartments, the radio carries his voice. For some of the families listening, it's the one place those names are said out loud. The archbishop's name is Oscar Romero, and when he was chosen, some expected him to keep quiet. Today, how he didn't.

Romero was a careful, bookish priest when he was made archbishop, and some in power were glad of it. Then, soon after, his friend Rutilio Grande, a Jesuit priest who worked among poor farm families, was shot and killed on a country road, along with others traveling with him. Romero went to see the bodies. Those who knew him say something changed in him that night. He began to speak. He spoke for the farmers whose land and lives were taken, for the families of the disappeared, for the poor his country had pushed to the edge. He spoke against killing by any side. He used the pulpit and the radio, and when the church's radio station was bombed, he kept preaching. There's a line in Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction." Dumb there means unable to speak. People came to call Romero the voice of the voiceless. On his last Sunday he spoke straight to the soldiers. Paraphrased: you are our brothers, and no soldier has to obey an order to kill that goes against the law of God. He begged them, in God's name, to stop the repression. The next evening he was saying Mass in the chapel of a hospital where he lived, near cancer patients cared for by sisters. As he finished his sermon and turned toward the altar, a gunman fired through the open chapel door. He fell at the altar. The Catholic Church has since named him a saint, and Christians beyond the Catholic Church remember him too.
screen: `A FRIEND KILLED ON A COUNTRY ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak for the voiceless once. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose story doesn't get told. A worker nobody notices. A patient in a hallway. Someone held somewhere, waiting. A person in a country that doesn't make the news. Hold one of them in mind, and say their situation to yourself plainly, as if you were reading it on the radio. Then think of one place you could say it out loud: a conversation, a letter, a meeting. If you pray, you can pray for them, by name if you know it. The bell holds the time.
Oscar Romero. An archbishop of San Salvador who spoke for the poor and the disappeared, and was shot while saying Mass.

Your line: the voice of the voiceless. Today, pass on one story that isn't being told: tell it to one person, or write it down for someone who can act. This week ran from a Birmingham jail cell to a hospital chapel: a mountaintop, a little light, open windows, old sentences lifted, a song in Taizé. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

where people heard his Sunday sermons
where he was shot at the altar

myth: Romero was outspoken from the day he became archbishop
he was careful and bookish; he began to speak after his friend Rutilio Grande was killed.
in the King James Proverbs, 'the dumb' means the foolish
it means those unable to speak.
Romero spoke to the soldiers on his last Sunday
he told them no soldier has to obey an order to kill that goes against the law of God.

fork.setup: you're the new archbishop. your friend, a priest who worked with poor farmers, has just been killed on a country road. what do you do?
options: stay quiet and keep the peace with those in power.
begin to speak, Sunday after Sunday, for the poor and the disappeared.
leave the country.
fork.reveal: Romero began to speak, from the pulpit and on the radio, reading out names that no one else would say.

original.note: Hebrew, in Proverbs 31:8: the mute, one who cannot speak — the King James 'dumb'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a political figure from a civil war.
what it means: a bishop who began to speak for the poor after his friend was killed, and was shot at the altar.
what a scholar hears: Proverbs 31:8, open thy mouth for the dumb, lived out on Sunday radio, and a martyr the Catholic Church now names a saint.

sources.ref: Life of Oscar Romero (standard biographies; his homilies)
